title: undo, at every level
goal: B3 Take back an edit, a staging, a commit or a push — each with the right tool
startWith: In git-lab. Make a mess deliberately at each level, then undo it.

newIdeas.plain: Undo in the working tree or the index. Touches no history.
Move the branch pointer. --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstages them, --hard throws them away.
A new commit that undoes an old one. The only safe undo for pushed history.

tasks.do: Throw away an uncommitted edit to one file
tasks.how: In IntelliJ this one is safer: Local History still has the edit after a rollback, git does not.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
echo 'oops' >> README.md
git restore README.md                    # gone, git cannot get it back
git restore --source=HEAD~1 README.md    # or take an older version

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
git add -A
git restore --staged .      # index cleared, edits intact

tasks.do: Undo the last commit three ways, and say which one you want
tasks.why: Same starting point, three very different results. Picking wrong is how work disappears.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
git reset --soft HEAD~1     # commit undone, changes still staged
git reset HEAD~1            # commit undone, changes unstaged (--mixed, the default)
git reset --hard HEAD~1     # commit and changes gone (the reflog can still save you)

tasks.do: Revert a pushed commit instead of resetting it
tasks.why: Reset rewrites history. On a branch other people have, that is their problem, not yours — revert instead.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
git revert <hash>
git revert --no-commit <hash1> <hash2>    # stack several into one commit

blocks.label: IntelliJ
blocks.body: Right-click a commit in the Log → Revert Commit. Same command, and it opens the commit dialog for the message.

tasks.why: The reflog records every position HEAD held for about 90 days. Almost nothing is truly lost.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
git reflog -20
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}        # back to where you were
git switch -c rescue <hash>      # or give the lost commit a branch

proof.expect: a list of recent HEAD moves
proof.note: You destroyed a commit and got it back.

doneWhen: “I think I lost work” is a two-minute reflog lookup, not a panic.

lessons.title: Rollback, and the net under it
lessons.teach: Ctrl+Alt+Z reverts a file to HEAD. Unlike git restore, the IDE still has the edit: right-click the file → Local History → Show History and take it back. Git never saw those versions at all.
lessons.fallbackTip: git restore <file> — and there is no undo for that one.
